errors.why: brtul zhugs bzang po renders Suvrata (good vow/observance), not Sucarita (good conduct, legs spyod).

note: A fluent, faithful rendering of the kāvya and the narrative; the Brahmin's name is the only real slip.

errors.english: it should be viewed as a consciousness that is a subversion of the essential nature as previously explained
errors.why: The Tibetan says ignorance should be seen as having, in nature, the erroneous cognition (viparyāsa-jñāna) described above, not a cognition that subverts an essential nature.

fix.find: it should be viewed as a consciousness that is a subversion of the essential nature as previously explained
fix.replace: it should be viewed as being, in nature, the erroneous cognition (viparyāsa-jñāna) explained above

note: The Daśabhūmika citation and the argument about ignorance and the view of self are followed correctly, apart from one misparsed definition.

errors.english: who sever the hopeless despair of living beings
errors.why: re thag gcod means to cut off (dash) beings' hope: by departing, the Sage leaves them hopeless, which is the opposite of removing their despair.

note: A good rendering of the lament verses (as prose); one line inverts the sense.

errors.english: for the purpose of reversing conceptual thought (kalpana) that perceives a contradictory nature
errors.why: The word non-mistaken excludes cognition that is FREE FROM conceptual thought (kalpanāpoḍha) yet grasps a contradictory nature; the translation drops 'free from' and has it exclude conceptual thought instead.

fix.find: for the purpose of reversing conceptual thought (kalpana) that perceives a contradictory nature
fix.replace: for the purpose of excluding cognition that is free from conceptual thought (kalpanā) yet grasps a contradictory nature

errors.why: dbyibs is saṃsthāna (shape); ākāra is rnam pa.

errors.english: Is this not done so that valid cognition (pramana) reliable knowledge or a valid means of knowing does not become mistaken?
errors.why: The objection is that the word serves to keep one from mistaking that cognition for a pramāṇa, not to keep pramāṇa from being mistaken.

errors.english: it follows the pupil of the eye
errors.why: It is the pupil of the eye that follows the rapidly whirled firebrand, not the firebrand that follows the pupil.

note: Generally readable, but the key point about what abhrānta excludes is reversed, and there are several smaller misreadings.
A faithful rendering of Avalokitavrata's gloss on the root verse and of the Sāṃkhya/Vaiśeṣika example of a statement open to censure.

errors.why: gdol pa is caṇḍāla (outcaste), as in the Lotus Sūtra's list of people to avoid, not hunters.

errors.english: Those who dwell in the teachings will ask how such qualities could possibly exist or not exist today, and even executioners will be sent forth.
errors.why: Those who abide in the dharmas are the targets (la): others, saying that such dharmas do not exist at all nowadays, will even dispatch executioners against them.

errors.english: we are seekers of virtue in name only, and possess no virtues of a seeker
errors.why: dge sbyong is śramaṇa (renunciant/ascetic); 'seeker of virtue' is a calque of the Tibetan, not the term.

note: The sūtra verses are mostly understood, but one passage misattributes who persecutes whom and the Lotus Sūtra list has a wrong term.
A faithful rendering of the Devadatta/Yajñadatta continuum argument, the opponent's dilemma and the reply.

errors.why: This is a Mūlasarvāstivāda text; the Sanskrit term is saṅghāvaśeṣa, not the Pali saṅghādisesa.

errors.english: It is because one contradicts the reality of the discipline.
errors.why: dngos po here refers to the Vinaya chapter (vastu) where the rule is stated: the reason is that it contradicts what the vastu says, not 'the reality of the discipline'.

note: The casuistry on offenses, purification by jñapti and confession is followed well; there is a Pali form and one misread reference to the vastu.

errors.english: those cognitions which appear as objects are not distinct from the objects even if external objects exist
errors.why: The verse says the appearing object and the cognition are not distinct, even if external objects exist (the commentary: the appearance of blue and its awareness are not separate).

fix.find: those cognitions which appear as objects are not distinct from the objects even if external objects exist
fix.replace: the appearing object and the cognition are not distinct from each other even if external objects exist

errors.english: the object of measurement is self-awareness, which is the result
errors.why: In Dharmakīrti's triad the self (grasping aspect) is the prameya and self-awareness is the result; the English collapses prameya into the result.
The Tibetan says only that object, means and result are established (when the self is posited as object); 'within the mind' is added.

note: The Pramāṇa argument on self-awareness and external objects is followed in outline, but the key verses on the pramāṇa-triad and on the non-difference of the appearing object and the cognition are misparsed.

errors.english: This rule does apply to all categories of downfalls such as theft
errors.why: The Tibetan says the rule does NOT apply to all classes of offense such as theft, only to killing.

fix.find: This rule does apply to all categories of downfalls such as theft
fix.replace: This rule does not apply to all categories of downfalls such as theft

errors.english: (payantika) an offense requiring confession and forfeiture
errors.why: ltung byed (pāyantika) requires confession only; forfeiture belongs to the naiḥsargika-pāyantika (spang ltung).

fix.find: (payantika) an offense requiring confession and forfeiture

errors.english: if a non-human is born from a human womb and possesses the lineage of a human
errors.why: The example (pārājika for theft from a human) requires a human born from a non-human womb, in line with the rule that a being belongs to its own realm.

errors.english: regarding those non-humans and animals who belong to the human realm or take on the physical forms of others
errors.why: The phrase is about one belonging to the human realm who displays the bodily form of the other realms (non-human, animal).

note: The realm-of-birth and assumed-form casuistry is mostly clear, but a lost negation reverses the scope of the rule, and the pāyantika gloss is wrong.
